what_it_does: Modern processors run many small tasks in parallel, using a scheduler to hand each task to whichever core is free. The problem is that a task often reads data that was just written by a previous task, and if those two tasks run on different cores, the second one suffers a costly main-memory fetch that a nearby core could have avoided. This paper builds a tiny hardware accelerator that continuously figures out which tasks share data and should therefore run on the same core, completing that analysis in under 300 clock cycles — up to 581 times faster than equivalent software — and using its suggestions to direct tasks toward their optimal cores, cutting execution time by up to 50%.
method_in_detail:
The problem. When a task finishes, the data it wrote sits warm in that core's private cache. If the next task that needs that data goes to a different core, it must fetch from main memory — a trip that can cost hundreds of clock cycles. Standard schedulers just send ready tasks to any idle core, ignoring this locality entirely. Telling programmers to manually pin tasks to cores is fragile and hard to maintain.

The idea. The paper treats the set of in-flight tasks as a graph, where an edge connects two tasks that share data. It then runs a well-known graph-clustering algorithm called label propagation (LP) on that graph in real time. LP works by giving each node a label, then repeatedly having each node adopt whatever label its neighbors use most — like a room of people gradually agreeing on a slogan. Nodes that are densely connected converge to the same label, forming a cluster. The paper maps each cluster to one processor core, so data-sharing tasks land on the same core and find their inputs already warm in cache.

How it works — the hardware. A dedicated chip (Task-LP) keeps a compact 128-by-128 bitmask adjacency matrix encoding which tasks share data. When a new dependency arrives, Task-LP restarts its LP computation. It can process multiple tasks and multiple label candidates in parallel each cycle, using bitwise AND plus a popcount (a fast bit-counting operation) to evaluate label popularity. A graph-coloring scheme ensures only independent tasks are updated simultaneously, guaranteeing convergence. The whole computation typically finishes in under 300 cycles.

Balancing locality and utilization. Pure locality enforcement can leave cores idle. The Task Placement Engine (TPE) wraps Task-LP and adds a tunable relaxation parameter: an idle core with no preferred tasks may steal any task after waiting at most a few hundred cycles, keeping cores busy without abandoning the locality gains.

The result. On a 24-core RISC-V processor mapped to an FPGA, Task-LP cuts execution time by up to 1.50x across scientific workloads (matrix factorizations, sparse solvers) and reduces per-task data-cache misses by up to 1.81x. The hardware is also validated at scale on a 192-core cloud server, where LP-guided scheduling reaches a median 15.1x speedup over serial execution, compared to 9.5x for the random baseline.
